DETAILED ACTION
The communication dated 10/10/2022 has been entered and fully considered.
Claims 1-20 are currently pending.
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claim 20 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as failing to set forth the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant regards as the invention.
Claim 20 refers to the dishwasher appliance of claim 14, but there is no dishwasher appliance in claim 14.  Correction is required.  For the purposes of prosecution, examiner is determining that claim 20 is dependent on claim 16.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claims 1-2, 4-5, 8, and 13 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by over Prinz et al. U.S. Publication 2006/0114128 (henceforth referred to as Prinz).
As to claim 1, A control panel (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] operating device 10) for an appliance, the control panel defining a display direction (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] decorative panel 20 faces towards the user defining a display direction) and comprising:
a printed circuit board defining a first surface (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] circuit board 12), a second surface (FIG. 1  shows that there are at least two surfaces of circuit board 12) opposite the first surface along the display direction, and a through hole passing through the printed circuit board from the first surface to the second surface (FIG. 1 shows display elements 14 and carrier 18 going through circuit board 12);
a console cover mounted to the first surface of the printed circuit board (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] decorative panel 20);
a standoff feature (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] the horizontal portions of carrier 18 reads on the claimed standoff feature) positioned between the console cover and the printed circuit board to create a localized gap between the console cover and the printed circuit board (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] the horizontal portions of carrier 18 makes a space between circuit board 12 and decorative panel 20);

a retention feature that engages the second surface to retain the printed circuit board against the console cover (FIG. 5 paragraph [0039] latching hooks 24); and
an electronic component (paragraph [0029] integral functional module 22 combines components 16-18.  Integral functional module 22 reads on the claimed electronic component) mounted to the printed circuit board and having an electrical contact that extends through the through hole (FIGS. 1 and 5 paragraph [0029] integral functional module 22 can be used with operating device 10.  Integrated functional module 22 is mounted to circuit board 12), wherein a distal end of the electrical contact forms a connection joint that is positioned within the localized gap between the printed circuit board and the console cover (FIG. 1 display elements 14 on circuit board 12 are in contact with mechanical actuating elements 16 within the localized gap).
As to claim 2, Prinz further teaches the retention feature (FIG. 5 paragraph [0039] latching hooks 24) is defined proximate to the standoff feature and on an opposite side of the standoff feature relative to the localized gap (FIGS. 1 and 5 paragraph [0027] The horizontal portions of carrier 18 and latching hooks 24 are on opposite sides of carrier 18).
As to claim 4, Prinz further teaches the standoff feature (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] the horizontal portions of carrier 18 reads on the claimed standoff feature) is defined by and protrudes from the printed circuit board toward the console cover to create the localized gap between the console cover and the printed circuit board (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] the horizontal portions of carrier 18 makes a space between circuit board 12 and decorative panel 20).
As to claim 5, Prinz further teaches the standoff feature defines a contact surface that is angled relative to a cover direction (FIG. 1 the horizontal portions of carrier 18 are at a perpendicular angle relative to decorative panel 20), the cover direction being perpendicular to the display direction (the display direction is what the user sees.  Paragraph [0027] trim panel 20 is placed on the side of carrier 18 that faces the user. The trim panel is perpendicular to the display direction).
As to claim 8, Prinz further teaches the standoff feature is one of a plurality of standoff features (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] there are at least two horizontal portions of carrier 18) and the retention feature is one of a plurality of retention features (FIG. 5 paragraph [0039] plurality of latching hooks 24).
As to claim 13, Prinz further teaches a console bracket (FIG. 1 vertical portion of carrier 18 reads on the claimed console bracket), wherein the printed circuit board and the console cover are mounted to the console bracket (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] carrier 18 holds actuating elements 16 to circuit board 12.  The decorative trim panel 20 is placed on the other side of carrier 18), and wherein the console bracket defines the retention feature that contacts the second surface to retain the printed circuit board (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] vertical portion of carrier 18 is attached to the at least two horizontal portions of carrier 18).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 3, 6, and 9 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Prinz et al. U.S. Publication 2006/0114128 (henceforth referred to as Prinz).
As to claim 3, Prinz further teaches the standoff feature (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] the horizontal portions of carrier 18 reads on the claimed standoff feature).
Prinz does not teach a standoff feature that protrudes from the console cover toward the printed circuit board.  However, absent the demonstration of any new or unobvious results, the claimed configuration is considered by Examiner to be prima facie obvious as a rearrangement of parts. It is old and well known to rearrange parts, with no change in their respective functions, due to size/space design criteria, the manufacturing expense thereof or purely for aesthetics. See MPEP § 2144.04, VI, C. Rearrangement of Parts.
As to claim 6, Prinz further teaches the retention feature is a flexible clip (FIG. 5 paragraph [0039] latching hooks 24 come into snapping engagement with corresponding openings of the casing.  The latching hooks are flexible enough to snap into place.).
Prinz does not teach engaging the edge of the printed circuit board.  However, absent the demonstration of any new or unobvious results, the claimed configuration is considered by Examiner to be prima facie obvious as a rearrangement of parts. It is old and well known to rearrange parts, with no change in their respective functions, due to size/space design criteria, the manufacturing expense thereof or purely for aesthetics. See MPEP § 2144.04, VI, C. Rearrangement of Parts.
As to claim 9, Prinz further teaches the plurality of retention features (FIG. 5 paragraph [0039] plurality of latching hooks 24).
Prinz does not teach that the retention features are defined outside the plurality of standoff features relative to the localized gap.  However, absent the demonstration of any new or unobvious results, the claimed configuration is considered by Examiner to be prima facie obvious as a rearrangement of parts. It is old and well known to rearrange parts, with no change in their respective functions, due to size/space design criteria, the manufacturing expense thereof or purely for aesthetics. See MPEP § 2144.04, VI, C. Rearrangement of Parts.
Claims 7 and 12 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Prinz et al. U.S. Publication 2006/0114128 (henceforth referred to as Prinz) in view of Kim et al. U.S. Publication 2010/0177494 (henceforth referred to as Kim).
As to claim 7,  Prinz differs from the instant claim in failing to teach the printed circuit board defines a retention aperture, and wherein the retention feature passes through the retention aperture to engage the second surface of the printed circuit board.
Kim teaches a similar control panel (FIG. 1 paragraph [0041] control panel assembly 100).  Kim teaches the printed circuit board defines a retention aperture (FIG. 2 paragraph [0044] circuit board 400 is connected to guide member 300, which contains a hook reception parts 310 and 320.  Hook reception parts read on the claimed retention aperture), and wherein the retention feature (FIG. 2 paragraph [0045] hooks 210 and 220) passes through the retention aperture to engage the second surface of the printed circuit board (paragraph [0057] at least one hook reception part 310 and 320, receives at least one first hook 210 and 220 to assemble circuit board 400 to control panel 200).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the control panel as taught by Prinz with a retention aperture as taught by Kim.  It is known in the art to have apertures as it provides a surface that can be gripped by the retention portions (Prinz paragraph [0039]).  The apertures can also aid the control cover panel to be properly placed with the circuit board (Kim paragraph [0045]).
As to claim 12,  Kim further teaches the retention feature is defined by the console cover and protrudes from the console cover (FIG. 2 paragraph [0045] at least one hook 210 and 220 protrude from the rear surface of the control panel 200) toward the printed circuit board to contact the second surface to retain the printed circuit board (paragraph [0045] the hook 210 and 220 with the aid of guide member 300, allows for the assembly of control panel 200 and circuit board 400).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the control panel taught by Prinz with a retention feature that protrudes from the console cover as taught by Kim.   The retention feature allows the control panel 200 to assemble to circuit board 400 (paragraph [0045]).
Claims 10-11 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Prinz et al. U.S. Publication 2006/0114128 (henceforth referred to as Prinz) in view of Park et al. U.S. Publication 2014/0298865 (henceforth referred to as Park).
As to claim 10, Prinz differs from the instant claim in failing to teach the standoff feature defines a standoff height measured along the display direction, the standoff height being between about 0.01 inches and 0.25 inches.
Park teaches a similar control panel (FIG. 1 paragraph [0016] control panel CP).  Park teaches standoff feature defines a standoff height measured along the display direction, the standoff height being between about 0.01 inches and 0.25 inches (paragraph [0082] the interval between two parts may be increased to 7 millimeters or more by spacers 75.  Spacers 75 read on the claimed standoff feature and are used to create a height distance).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the control panel as taught by Prinz with a standoff height as taught by Park.  The use of spacers 75 are to prevent transmission of current between two parts (paragraph [0083]).  Since the art recognizes that the standoff height is a result effectively variable (enough to prevent current transmission), it would have been obvious to one skilled in the art to determine an optimal value for the standoff height in Prinz, through routine experimentation, and that the claimed heights would have been found obvious through such routine experimentation, unless the applicant can demonstrate unexpected results.
As to claim 11, Park further teaches the standoff height is about 0.03 inches (paragraph [0082] the interval can be increased to 7 millimeters or more.  This means the interval between two parts can be less than 7 millimeters).
Claims 14-15 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Prinz et al. U.S. Publication 2006/0114128 (henceforth referred to as Prinz) in view of Min et al. U.S. Publication 2017/0188787 (henceforth referred to as Min).
As to claim 14, Prinz further teaches the console cover comprises: a plurality of user input zones (paragraph [0012] decorative panel has corresponding openings for actuating elements and/or optical display elements); and a plurality of actuating elements mounted to the printed circuit board outside of the localized gap (FIG. 1 actuating elements 16 are outside the localized gap), the actuating elements being operable to detect user inputs via contact with the console cover in the plurality of user input zones (paragraph [0008] user inputs information to the control device via the control panel).
Prinz differs from the instant claim in failing to teach a capacitive sensor.
Min teaches a similar control panel (FIG. 2 paragraph [0061] operating unit 22).  Min teaches capacitive sensors (paragraph [0065] touch sensor 62 reads on the claimed capacitive sensors).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the control panel as taught by Prinz with capacitive sensors as taught by Min.  It is common the art to change actuators with capacitive-sensor style buttons.
As to claim 15, Min further teaches the control panel is mounted on a front panel or a top edge of a door of a dishwasher appliance (FIG. 1 paragraph [0061] operating unit 22 may be formed on upper surface of the door 20).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the control panel taught by Prinz be located at the upper surface of the door as taught by Min.  Having the control panel located at the top of the door makes it easier for users to see the panel and/or see the status of the dishwasher (paragraph [0037]).
Claims 16-19 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Prinz et al. U.S. Publication 2006/0114128 (henceforth referred to as Prinz) in view of Min et al. U.S. Publication 2017/0188787 (henceforth referred to as Min).
As to claim 16,  Prinz teaches control panel (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] operating device 10) comprising a printed circuit board defining a first surface (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] circuit board 12), a second surface (FIG. 1  shows that there are at least two surfaces of circuit board 12) opposite the first surface along the display direction (FIG. 1 decorative panel 20 is facing the user defining the display direction), and a through hole passing through the printed circuit board from the first surface to the second surface (FIG. 1 shows display elements 14 and carrier 18 going through circuit board 12);
a console cover mounted to the first surface of the printed circuit board (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] decorative panel 20);
a standoff feature (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] the horizontal portions of carrier 18 reads on the claimed standoff feature) positioned between the console cover and the printed circuit board to create a localized gap between the console cover and the printed circuit board (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] the horizontal portions of carrier 18 makes a space between circuit board 12 and decorative panel 20);
a retention feature (FIG. 5 paragraph [0039] latching hooks 24) that engages the second surface to retain the printed circuit board against the console cover;
and an electronic component (paragraph [0029] integral functional module 22 combines components 16-18.  Integral functional module 22 reads on the claimed electronic component) mounted to the printed circuit board and having an electrical contact that extends through the through hole (FIGS. 1 and 5 paragraph [0029] integral functional module 22 can be used with operating device 10.  Integrated functional module 22 is mounted to circuit board 12), wherein a distal end of the electrical contact forms a connection joint that is positioned within the localized gap between the printed circuit board and the console cover (FIG. 1 display elements 14 on circuit board 12 are in contact with mechanical actuating elements 16 within the localized gap).
Prinz differs from the instant claim in failing to teach a dishwasher appliance defining a vertical direction, a lateral direction, and a transverse direction, the dishwasher appliance comprising:
a wash tub positioned within a cabinet and defining a wash chamber;
a door pivotally mounted to the cabinet to provide selective access to the wash chamber;
and a control panel mounted on the door and defining a display direction.
Min teaches a dishwasher appliance (FIG. 1 paragraph [0056] dish washer 1).  Min teaches a dishwasher appliance defining a vertical direction, a lateral direction, and a transverse direction (FIG. 1 the dishwasher is a three-dimensional appliance), the dishwasher appliance comprising:
a wash tub positioned within a cabinet and defining a wash chamber (paragraph [0057] a tub is provided inside cabinet 10);
a door pivotally mounted to the cabinet (FIG. 1 paragraph [0059] door 20 is rotatably mounted on front of cabinet 10) to provide selective access to the wash chamber (paragraph [0058] the door 20 can be opened and closed to expose the tub inside cabinet 10);
and a control panel mounted on the door and defining a display direction (FIG. 1 paragraph [0061] operating unit 22 may be formed on upper surface of the door 20).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to combine the control panel taught by Prinz with the dishwasher as taught by Min.  It is known in the art to have a control panel to control the operations of a dishwasher (Min paragraph [0080]).
As to claim 17,  Prinz further teaches the retention feature (FIG. 5 paragraph [0039] latching hooks 24) is defined proximate to the standoff feature and on an opposite side of the standoff feature relative to the localized gap (FIGS. 1 and 5 paragraph [0027] The horizontal portions of carrier 18 and latching hooks 24 are on opposite sides of carrier 18).
As to claim 18, Prinz further teaches the standoff feature (FIG. 1 paragraph [0027] the horizontal portions of carrier 18 reads on the claimed standoff feature).
Prinz does not teach a standoff feature that protrudes from the console cover toward the printed circuit board.  However, absent the demonstration of any new or unobvious results, the claimed configuration is considered by Examiner to be prima facie obvious as a rearrangement of parts. It is old and well known to rearrange parts, with no change in their respective functions, due to size/space design criteria, the manufacturing expense thereof or purely for aesthetics. See MPEP § 2144.04, VI, C. Rearrangement of Parts.
As to claim 19, Prinz further teaches the standoff feature defines a contact surface that is angled relative to a cover direction (FIG. 1 the horizontal portions of carrier 18 are at a perpendicular angle relative to decorative panel 20), the cover direction being perpendicular to the display direction (the display direction is what the user sees.  Paragraph [0027] trim panel 20 is placed on the side of carrier 18 that faces the user. The trim panel is perpendicular to the display direction).
Claim 20 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Prinz et al. U.S. Publication 2006/0114128 (henceforth referred to as Prinz) and Min et al. U.S. Publication 2017/0188787 (henceforth referred to as Min) as applied to claim 16 above, and in further view of Kim et al. U.S. Publication 2010/0177494 (henceforth referred to as Kim).
As to claim 20, Prinz and Min differ from the instant claim in failing to teach the retention feature is defined by the console cover and protrudes from the console cover toward the printed circuit board to contact the second surface to retain the printed circuit board.
Kim teaches a similar control panel (FIG. 1 paragraph [0041] control panel assembly 100).  Kim teaches the retention feature is defined by the console cover and protrudes from the console cover (FIG. 2 paragraph [0045] at least one hook 210 and 220 protrude from the rear surface of the control panel 200) toward the printed circuit board to contact the second surface to retain the printed circuit board (paragraph [0045] the hook 210 and 220 with the aid of guide member 300, allows for the assembly of control panel 200 and circuit board 400).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the control panel taught by Prinz and Min with a retention feature that protrudes from the console cover as taught by Kim.   The retention feature allows the control panel 200 to assemble to circuit board 400 (paragraph [0045]).
Conclusion
